title: You forgot
hook: when troubled, you've forgotten that each person's mind shares in the divine (Meditations 12.26)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was calm water: drop the label, find the bay. Your line was in my power.

You walk into the kitchen and stand there. Why did you come in? You knew a second ago. Marcus thought being upset is a lot like that: not that you never knew the truth, but that it slipped out of your hand on the way in. So in book twelve he writes himself a list, not of new ideas, but of things he already knew and kept forgetting the moment someone annoyed him.
screen: `WHY DID I COME IN HERE?` → `NOT NEW IDEAS. OLD ONES, DROPPED.` → `YOU FORGOT.`

segments.voice: Meditations 12.26 opens, in plain words: when you're troubled by something, you've forgotten. Then he lists what. First, the list. You've forgotten that all things happen by the nature of the whole. That another person's wrong is theirs, not yours. That what's happening now has happened before and will again. That you're kin to every human being, not by blood or seed but by sharing in mind. Even yesterday's line is there: everything is opinion. Second, the line at the center: each person's mind, he says, is a god, and has flowed from there. The Greek word for mind is nous. For the Stoics, a divine reason runs through the whole world, and every human mind is a piece of it, a spark from the same fire. Readers take this differently. Some hear something close to religious faith. Some hear a poetic way of saying every person can reason, and so deserves respect. Marcus himself sometimes isn't sure what runs the world, as we saw a few days ago. Third, why it's in a list about being troubled. If the person who cut you off in traffic carries the same spark you do, your anger is aimed at a relative, a cousin in reason. That doesn't excuse what they did. It changes who you think you're dealing with. Fourth, the comfort in the word forgot. You don't need to become someone new. You need to remember what you already knew, which is why Marcus kept writing it down.
screen: `WHEN TROUBLED, YOU'VE FORGOTTEN.` · `EACH MIND SHARES IN THE DIVINE.` · `YOUR ANGER IS AIMED AT A RELATIVE.` · `REMEMBER, DON'T REINVENT.` · then, large: `I FORGOT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who's been hard to deal with lately, and try Marcus's reminder on them: this person has a mind, a spark of the same reason that's in you; they worry, they plan, they get things wrong. If you hold something sacred, let that word sit beside them for a moment; if you don't, let the word kin sit there, and notice whether anything shifts.
You forgot. Marcus's line for every troubled moment: you didn't lack the truth, you dropped it, including that each person's mind shares in the divine. Today's word.
Your line: I forgot. Remembering again is enough; you don't need anything new. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 634 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A SMALL SHARE OF TIME.`

howItsDone: Readers of the Meditations often use 12.26 as a checklist when upset, running through Marcus's reminders, among them that every person's mind shares in the same reason.

fork.reveal: Marcus says when we're troubled we've forgotten our kinship: a community of mind, not of blood.

original.note: Greek: mind, intelligence. Marcus says each person's nous is a god, flowed from the whole.

chat.says: Why does Marcus say being upset means I've forgotten something?
options: Because you already knew the reminders: others' wrongs are theirs, and we're kin in mind.
Because getting upset means you skipped a lesson and must learn it from scratch.
Because he thought upset people forget the facts of what really happened to them.
chat.meaning: In 12.26 Marcus says the troubled person has forgotten things already known: the whole, that others' wrongs are theirs, and kinship in mind.

nous.meaning: Greek for mind; for Marcus, each mind flows from the divine

Stoics.meaning: followers of Stoicism, the Greek school of philosophy Marcus followed

Meditations.meaning: the private notebook of reflections Marcus Aurelius wrote to himself

notes: 12.26 paraphrased; confirm the reminders listed (universal nature; another's wrong; it has always happened so; kinship by intelligence not blood or seed; each mind a god and an efflux of the deity). Count deliberately left vague ('several').

'Spark from the same fire' is an explanatory image, not Marcus's wording in 12.26.
